summary: Registers the MIME types associated with the 3GPP multimedia file format, which belongs to the family based on the ISO Media File Format. Registration lets software identify and handle these audio and video files on the Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3839 registers the two MIME media types for 3GPP multimedia files. A file served as video/3gpp or audio/3gpp tells any server or mail program what kind of data it is holding, and the registration says how the file must be encoded and how to recognise it.

subtitle: The media types that mark a file as 3GPP multimedia, so a server can serve it correctly.

tldr.problem: The 3GPP file format holds the audio and video that mobile phones download, but nothing in the wider Internet said which media type a 3GP file should carry, so a server had no standard label to put in a Content-Type header.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers two media types, audio/3gpp and video/3gpp, with the parameters, encoding rules and file identification that each needs, and requires that the file carry a 3GPP brand in its compatible brands list.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3839 is a Proposed Standard from July 2004 and has been updated by RFC 6381.

today: RFC 3839 is a Proposed Standard from July 2004 and has been updated by RFC 6381. The media types audio/3gpp and video/3gpp remain the standard labels for 3GPP multimedia files.

sections.title: The 3GP File Format and Its Brands
sections.content:
The third-generation partnership project, 3GPP, has defined a standard file format for the audio and visual sequences that may be downloaded to cellular phones. At the time of writing, the 3GPP file format, 3GP, can contain H.263 or MPEG-4 video, AMR narrow-band speech, AMR wide-band speech or AAC audio, and 3GPP timed text.

Like all files in the ISO family, a 3GP file has an intrinsic file-type box at its start. That box identifies the specifications the file complies with, and it says which players, which may comply with only one specification, the content author permits to play the file. The identification is made with four-letter brands.

Files identified by the media types defined in this RFC must contain a brand defined in a 3GPP standard that can apply to 3GPP files, in their compatible brands list. The media types are needed to identify such files correctly when they are served over HTTP, included in multipart documents, or used in other places where media types are used.
sections.plainLanguage: A 3GP file starts with a box that names the standards it follows, using four-letter brands. The media type is the second half of the identification: it tells a server or a mail program what kind of file it is holding.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The 3GPP file format may contain audio, video and displayable text data. There is currently no provision for active elements such as scripts of any kind.

It is clearly possible to author malicious files that call for an excessively large picture size or high sampling-rate audio. Clients can and usually do protect themselves against this kind of attack.

The RFC notes that selected metadata fields may hold information intended to protect the media against unauthorised use or distribution. In that case the intention is that altering or removing the data in the field would be treated as an offence under national agreements based on World Intellectual Property Organization treaties.

The 3GPP files have an extensible structure, so in theory metadata fields or media formats could be defined in the future that induce particular actions on the part of the recipient, and so present additional security risks. That kind of capability is not supported in the referenced specification at present. There is also no provision in the standards for encryption, signing or authentication of these file formats.
sections.plainLanguage: The format holds media and text, with nothing that runs. A file can still be built to be expensive to open, and the format has no way to encrypt or sign what it carries.

sections.title: The Two Registered Media Types
sections.content:
The registration applies to all files defined as using the 3GP file format and identified with a suitable brand in a 3GPP specification. The usual file suffix for all of them is '.3gp'.

The type audio/3gpp may be used for files that contain audio but no visual presentation, neither video nor timed text. The type video/3gpp is valid for all files, and it is valid to serve an audio-only file as video/3gpp.

Both registrations share the same shape. Neither has required or optional parameters at the time of writing, though the RFC notes that ongoing work may introduce optional parameters, and gives one example area of effort: a parameter that would let the codecs in use within the media type be asserted and determined without examining the file. The files are binary and should be transmitted in a suitable encoding without CR and LF conversion or 7-bit stripping, and base64 is a suitable encoding. The RFC stresses that these media types are used only for files: separate types are used for real-time transfer, such as the RTP payload format for AMR audio and the RTP payload formats for H.263.

Both registrations name the same published specifications, 3GPP 26.234 Release 5 and 3GPP 26.244 Release 6 or later, note that the 3GPP organisation has defined the specification, interoperability and conformance and conducts regular interoperability testing, and list multi-media as the application. The contact for further information is the Nokia MIME manager, the intended usage is COMMON, and the change controller is 3GPP.
sections.plainLanguage: One type is for sound-only files and the other for anything. Both carry no parameters, both travel as base64 in mail, and both are managed by 3GPP.

sections.title: The audio/3gpp Registration in Detail
sections.content:
The media type name is audio and the subtype name is 3gpp. The registration adds two conditions on use. The type may be used for files that contain audio but no visual presentation, and files served under this type must not contain any visual material. The RFC notes that 3GPP timed text is visually presented and is therefore counted as visual material.

There are no magic numbers as such, but the file-type box must occur first in the file and must contain a 3GPP brand in its compatible brands list. The file extensions 3gp and 3gpp are both declared at the NIST registry, with 3gp preferred. The Macintosh file type code is 3gpp.
sections.plainLanguage: The sound-only type is for files with no visual content at all, and timed text counts as visual. There is no fixed byte pattern to look for, but the file must open with the file-type box and a 3GPP brand in it.

sections.title: The video/3gpp Registration in Detail
sections.content:
The media type name is video and the subtype name is 3gpp. This type is valid for all files, so an audio-only file may be served under it as well.

As with the audio type, there are no magic numbers, but the file-type box must occur first in the file and must contain a 3GPP brand in its compatible brands list. The file extensions 3gp and 3gpp are both declared at the NIST registry, with 3gp preferred, and the Macintosh file type code is 3gpp.
sections.plainLanguage: The general type covers every 3GP file, whatever is inside it. The same file-type box rule applies, and the same file extensions.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The document registers the media types audio/3gpp and video/3gpp with IANA, as defined above.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the list of media types, and this RFC adds the two 3GPP entries to it.

cells: No, timed text counts as visual material
